blocks.p: So I saw that Christian went on his way. Yet at the sight of the old man sitting in the mouth of the cave, he did not know what to think, especially because the old man spoke to him, though he could not come after him. “You will never mend,” he said, “until more of you are burned.” But Christian held his peace, put a bold face on it, and so went by without harm. Then Christian sang:

v: O world of wonders! I can say no less,
that I should be preserved in such
distress
as I have met with here! O blessed be
the hand that from it has delivered me!
Dangers in darkness, devils, hell, and
sin
surrounded me while I this vale was in;
yes, snares and pits and traps and nets
all lay
about my path, so that, in my weak way,
I might have been caught, tangled, and cast down;
but since I live, let JESUS wear the crown.

blocks.p: Now, as Christian went on his way, he came to a little rise, which had been built up on purpose so that pilgrims could see ahead of them. Christian climbed it, and looking forward, he saw Faithful ahead of him on his journey.
“Hey! Hey! Hello there!” Christian called out loud. “Wait, and I’ll be your companion!”
At that, Faithful looked behind him, and Christian called again, “Wait, wait until I catch up with you!”

But Faithful answered, “No, I’m running for my life, and the avenger of blood is behind me.” This stung Christian a little, and putting all his strength into it, he quickly caught up with Faithful, and even ran past him, so that the last was first. Then Christian smiled with vain pride, because he had gotten ahead of his brother. But not watching his feet, he suddenly stumbled and fell, and could not get up again until Faithful came up and helped him.
Then I saw in my dream that they went on together very lovingly, and had sweet conversation about everything that had happened to them on their pilgrimage. Christian began like this:
“My honored and dearly loved brother Faithful, I’m glad I’ve caught up with you, and that God has so tuned our spirits that we can walk as companions on this pleasant road.”
“I had hoped, dear friend, to have your company all the way from our town. But you got the start on me, so I was forced to come this far alone.”
“How long did you stay in the City of Destruction before you set out after me on your pilgrimage?”
“Until I couldn’t stay any longer. Soon after you left, there was a great deal of talk that before long our city would be burned to the ground with fire from heaven.”
“What! Did our neighbors talk like that?”
“Yes. For a while it was on everyone’s lips.”
“What! And no one but you came out to escape the danger?”

“Though there was a great deal of talk about it, as I said, I don’t think they really believed it. In the heat of the conversation I heard some of them speak mockingly of you and your desperate journey, for that’s what they called your pilgrimage. But I believed, and still do, that our city will end in fire and brimstone from above; and so I have made my escape.”
“Didn’t you hear any talk of our neighbor Pliable?”
“Yes, Christian. I heard that he followed you until he came to the Swamp of Despair, where, as some said, he fell in. He wouldn’t admit to it, but I’m sure he was well smeared with that kind of mud.”
“And what did the neighbors say to him?”

“Since he came back, he’s been held in great contempt, by all sorts of people. Some mock and despise him, and hardly anyone will give him work. He’s seven times worse off now than if he had never left the city.”
“But why should they be so set against him, since they also despise the way he abandoned?”

“Oh, they say, ‘Hang him, he’s a turncoat! He wasn’t true to what he professed.’ I think God has stirred up even his enemies to hiss at him and make him a byword, because he has forsaken the way.” [Jer. 29:18-19]
“Didn’t you talk with him before you came out?”
“I met him once in the street, but he slunk off to the other side, like someone ashamed of what he had done. So I didn’t speak to him.”

“Well,” said Christian, “when I first set out, I had hopes of that man. But now I’m afraid he’ll perish when the city is overthrown. It has happened to him just as the true proverb says: ‘A dog returns to its vomit, and a sow that is washed goes back to wallowing in the mud.’” [2 Pet. 2:22]
“That’s my fear for him too. But who can stop what is going to be?”

“Well, neighbor Faithful,” said Christian, “let’s leave him and talk about things that concern us more directly. Tell me now what you’ve met with on the road as you came. I know you’ve met with some things, or else it ought to be written down as a wonder.”
“I escaped the swamp that I see you fell into, and got up to the gate without that danger. Only I met with a woman named Wanton, who very nearly did me harm.”
“It’s good you escaped her net. Joseph was hard pressed by her, and he escaped her as you did; but it nearly cost him his life. [Gen. 39:11-13] But what did she do to you?”
“You can’t imagine, unless you already know something of it, what a flattering tongue she had. She pressed me hard to turn aside with her, promising me every kind of contentment.”
“No, she didn’t promise you the contentment of a good conscience.”
“You know what I mean: every kind of bodily, sensual contentment.”
“Thank God you escaped her. ‘The one the Lord is angry with will fall into her pit.’” [Prov. 22:14]
“No, I’m not sure whether I escaped her completely or not.”
“Why? Surely you didn’t give in to her desires?”

“No, not to defile myself; for I remembered an old writing I had seen, which said, ‘Her steps lead straight to hell.’ [Prov. 5:5] So I shut my eyes, so that I would not be bewitched by her looks. [Job 31:1] Then she cursed me, and I went on my way.”
“Didn’t you meet any other attack as you came?”

“When I came to the foot of the hill called Difficulty, I met a very old man, who asked me who I was and where I was going. I told him I was a pilgrim on my way to the Celestial City. Then the old man said, ‘You look like an honest fellow. Would you be willing to live with me, for the wages I will give you?’ I asked him his name and where he lived. He said his name was Adam the First, and that he lived in the town of Deceit. [Eph. 4:22] I asked him what his work was, and what wages he would pay. He told me his work was many pleasures, and his wages were that I should be his heir in the end. I asked him further what kind of house he kept, and what other servants he had. He told me his house was stocked with all the delicacies in the world, and that his servants were his own offspring. Then I asked if he had any children. He said he had only three daughters, the Lust of the Flesh, the Lust of the Eyes, and the Pride of Life, and that I could marry them all if I liked. [1 John 2:16] Then I asked how long he wanted me to live with him, and he told me, as long as he lived himself.”
“Well, and what conclusion did you and the old man come to in the end?”

“Why, at first I found myself somewhat inclined to go with the man, for I thought he spoke very fairly. But looking at his forehead as I talked with him, I saw written there, ‘Put off the old man and his deeds.’”
“And then?”

“Then it came burning hot into my mind that whatever he said, and however he flattered, once he got me home to his house he would sell me as a slave. So I told him to stop talking, for I would not come near the door of his house. Then he cursed me, and told me he would send someone after me who would make my road bitter to my soul. So I turned to leave him. But just as I turned to go, I felt him take hold of my flesh and give me such a deadly wrench backward that I thought he had torn part of me away with him. This made me cry out, ‘O wretched man!’ [Rom. 7:24] So I went on my way up the hill.
“When I had gotten about halfway up, I looked behind me and saw someone coming after me as swift as the wind. He caught up with me just about where the bench stands.”
“Right there,” said Christian, “is where I sat down to rest; but being overcome with sleep, I lost this scroll from inside my coat.”

“But, good brother, hear me out. As soon as the man caught up with me, it was a word and a blow, for he knocked me down and left me for dead. When I came to myself a little, I asked him why he treated me like that. He said it was because of my secret leaning toward Adam the First; and with that he struck me another deadly blow on the chest and knocked me over backward, so that I lay at his feet as dead as before. When I came to myself again, I begged him for mercy; but he said, ‘I don’t know how to show mercy,’ and with that he knocked me down again. He would surely have finished me off, except that someone came by and told him to stop.”
“Who was it that told him to stop?”
“I didn’t know him at first; but as he went by, I saw the holes in his hands and in his side, and then I knew he was our Lord. So I went on up the hill.”
“The man who overtook you was Moses. He spares no one, and he doesn’t know how to show mercy to those who break his law.”

“I know that very well. It wasn’t the first time he had come after me. He was the one who came to me when I was living comfortably at home, and told me he would burn my house down over my head if I stayed there.”
“But didn’t you see the house that stood there at the top of the hill, on the side of which Moses met you?”

“Yes, and the lions too, before I got to it. But as for the lions, I think they were asleep, for it was about noon; and since I had so much of the day ahead of me, I went past the porter and came down the hill.”

“He told me he saw you go by. But I wish you had stopped at the house, for they would have shown you so many treasures that you would hardly have forgotten them to the day you die. But tell me, did you meet anyone in the Valley of Humiliation?”

“Yes, I met a man named Discontent, who would gladly have persuaded me to go back with him. His reason was that the valley was entirely without honor. He told me, besides, that going there was the way to offend all my friends, such as Pride, Arrogance, Self-Conceit, Worldly-Glory, and others, who he knew, so he said, would be very much offended if I made such a fool of myself as to wade through this valley.”
“Well, and how did you answer him?”

“I told him that although all those he named might claim kinship with me, and rightly, since they were indeed my relatives by nature, yet since I became a pilgrim they have disowned me, as I have rejected them; and so now they were no more to me than if they had never been of my family. I told him, moreover, that he had completely misrepresented this valley: for humility comes before honor, and a proud spirit before a fall. So, I said, I would rather go through this valley to the honor that the wisest count as honor, than choose what he thought most worthy of our love.”
“Did you meet nothing else in that valley?”

“Yes, I met Shame. But of all the men I met on my pilgrimage, he, I think, has the wrong name. The others would take no for an answer after a little argument and so on; but this bold-faced Shame would never give up.”
“Why, what did he say to you?”

“What! Why, he raised objections against religion itself. He said it was a pitiful, low, sneaking business for a man to concern himself with religion. He said a tender conscience was an unmanly thing, and that for a man to watch his words and ways, tying himself down from the swaggering freedom that the bold spirits of the day are used to, would make him the laughingstock of the age. He objected, too, that few of the powerful, rich, or wise were ever of my opinion [1 Cor. 1:26; 3:18; Phil. 3:7-8], nor any of them at all [John 7:48], until they were persuaded to become fools and, of their own free will, risk the loss of everything for who knows what. He objected besides to the low and humble condition of most of the pilgrims of every age, and to their ignorance and lack of understanding in all the natural sciences.

“He kept at me like that about a great many more things than I’m telling you: that it was a shame to sit whimpering and mourning under a sermon, and a shame to come home sighing and groaning; that it was a shame to ask my neighbor’s forgiveness for little faults, or to pay back what I had taken from anyone. He said, too, that religion makes a man a stranger to the great because of a few vices, which he called by finer names, and makes him acknowledge and respect the lowly simply because they belong to the same religious brotherhood. ‘And isn’t that,’ he said, ‘a shame?’”
“And what did you say to him?”

“Say! At first I didn’t know what to say. He pressed me so hard that the blood rushed to my face; this very Shame brought it up, and very nearly beat me off altogether. But at last I began to consider that ‘what people value highly is detestable in God’s sight.’ [Luke 16:15] And I thought again: this Shame tells me what men are, but nothing about what God is, or what the Word of God is. I thought, moreover, that on the Day of Judgment we will not be sentenced to death or to life according to the swaggering spirits of the world, but according to the wisdom and law of the Most High. So, I thought, what God says is best is best indeed, even if every man in the world is against it.

“Seeing, then, that God prefers his religion; seeing that God prefers a tender conscience; seeing that those who make themselves fools for the kingdom of heaven are the wisest; and that the poor man who loves Christ is richer than the greatest man in the world who hates him: Shame, get out! You are an enemy to my salvation. Shall I take your side against my sovereign Lord? Then how could I look him in the face when he comes? If I were ashamed of his ways and his servants now, how could I expect his blessing? [Mark 8:38]

“But this Shame was a bold villain. I could hardly shake him off. He kept haunting me, continually whispering in my ear about one or another of the weaknesses that come with religion. But at last I told him it was useless to try any further, for the very things he despised were the things in which I saw the most glory. And so at last I got past this persistent one. And when I had shaken him off, I began to sing:

v: The trials faced by those who hear the call
from heaven, and obey it, are not small:
they’re many, and they’re suited to the flesh,
and come, and come, and come again afresh,
so that, if not today, some other day,
we may be taken, beaten, cast away.
Oh, let the pilgrims, let the pilgrims, then,
be watchful, and conduct themselves like men.”

blocks.p: “I’m glad, my brother, that you stood up to this villain so bravely,” said Christian. “I agree, of all of them, I think he has the wrong name. He’s so bold as to follow us in the streets and try to put us to shame in front of everyone, that is, to make us ashamed of what is good. If he weren’t so brazen himself, he would never try what he does. But let’s keep resisting him; for in spite of all his bluster, he promotes the fool and no one else. ‘The wise inherit honor,’ said Solomon, ‘but fools get only shame.’” [Prov. 3:35]
“I think we must cry for help against Shame to the One who wants us to be brave for the truth on the earth.”
“That’s true. But did you meet anyone else in that valley?”
“No, not I. I had sunshine all the rest of the way through it, and through the Valley of the Shadow of Death as well.”

“That was good for you. I’m sure it went far otherwise with me. Almost as soon as I entered that valley, I had a long and dreadful fight with that foul fiend Apollyon. I truly thought he would kill me, especially when he got me down and crushed me under him, as though he would crush me to pieces; for as he threw me, my sword flew out of my hand, and he told me he was sure of me. But I cried to God, and he heard me, and delivered me out of all my troubles. Then I entered the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and had no light for almost half the way through it. I thought I would be killed there over and over again; but at last the day broke and the sun rose, and I went through the rest with far more ease and quiet.”
